posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring compliance pain post with three senior ICP prospects engaging — validate the audit trail problem as structural, not a ChatGPT-specific issue, to position explainability as the real gap
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' problem is actually the 'black box said so' problem — it's been sitting in analytics for years, GPT just made it impossible to ignore. Regulators don't care how smart your model is, they care whether you can reconstruct the answer step by step on a Tuesday morning under pressure. Most tools aren't built for that conversation. Wonder how many teams are quietly in the same boat but haven't hit the audit yet.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person firm hitting the adoption wall with Power BI — validate the trust problem specifically, add the insight that it's a credibility gap not a tool gap
posts.draft_comment: The trust gap is the real product. Finance teams didn't stop trusting Excel — they just never had a reason to stop trusting it. A dashboard that can't explain where a number came from, or why it changed last Tuesday, will always lose to a spreadsheet someone built themselves. How long did it take before anyone even admitted that was the actual problem?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post that validates the 'less is more' dashboard philosophy — validate the insight with a specific observation, add the 'why it happens' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is almost always a trust problem disguised as a measurement problem — nobody could agree on what mattered, so everything made the list. The 10% usage stat is the tell. When people don't believe a dashboard will actually help them, they just stop opening it. Curious what the five metrics were that finally stuck.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail engaging on a post about BI chaos and ownership — validate the 'who owns truth' pain, add the insight that tooling is a red herring when governance is missing
posts.draft_comment: The three definitions of revenue thing is so common it's almost a rite of passage. The real issue isn't the tool — it's that most orgs hand people a licence before they've agreed on what anything actually means. Self-service works fine when there's a shared foundation underneath it. Who in your org is actually empowered to set that?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing AI hallucinations as a security risk — validate the reframe, add the overlooked trust layer, with a CEO prospect (Andrew Mills) in the thread who likely feels this acutely
posts.draft_comment: The reframe from accuracy problem to security problem is the right one — and honestly overdue. Most teams are still treating hallucinated outputs like a spell-check miss, not a liability. The scarier version isn't the report with obviously wrong numbers. It's the one that's 95% right.

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with BI frustration post — validate the £200k ghost-platform pain, add the real reason it happens, leave her thinking
posts.draft_comment: That £200k platform isn't broken — it's just built for someone who thinks in SQL, not someone who needs to know if margins are down before Thursday's call. The 'self-service' label does a lot of heavy lifting to cover that gap. The honest version would be: self-service for analysts, assisted-service for everyone else. How many of your clients have a BI tool that's basically just one person's personal dashboard at this point?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial firm hits the real root cause of BI failure — validate the culture diagnosis and add the layer that filters are a symptom, not the disease
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, same dataset, three answers — that's not a filter problem, that's a 'nobody agreed on what the question was' problem. The culture piece is right, but I'd go one step further: most orgs build dashboards before they've agreed on definitions. What does 'revenue' mean in your company? Ask five people and see how many answers you get. The CFO moment you're describing isn't a BI failure, it's just when the disagreement finally becomes visible.

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the 'nobody knows what to ask' adoption problem — validate that insight and reframe it as a data literacy gap, not a tooling problem
posts.draft_comment: That 12% number is painfully common — and I'd bet the 88% aren't lazy, they just don't have a mental model of what good looks like with these tools. The shadow ChatGPT usage is the tell. When people go off-platform on their phones, they're not avoiding AI — they're avoiding the friction of having to already know the answer before they can ask the question. What did onboarding actually look like for those 500 users?
